title: I am the worst of all
hookLine: Kabir says he is the worst, and everyone else is good (Kabir salok, ang 1364)

cards: A group chat goes sour. Someone said something careless, someone else snapped, and now everyone is typing out exactly who did what wrong. Screenshots.
Receipts. Every message pointing outward. Now set beside that scene a couplet, two short lines, from the back of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Kabir's saloks are gathered.
It points the other way entirely, so bluntly it can sound almost wrong on first hearing.

teach.h: I AM THE WORST OF ALL.
teach.b: Here's the salok. Kabir, it begins, I am the worst of all; apart from me, everyone is good. And the second line: whoever comes to see it this way is my friend.
That's the whole of it. It would be easy to hear this as someone who hates himself. Sikh teachers read it differently.
They hear humility, the low, open place where water gathers. Kabir isn't keeping a score where he loses. He's refusing to keep the score at all.

In that group chat, the eye points outward, to everyone else's faults, because that's where it naturally goes. Farid's couplet, a little over two weeks back on this path, said look inside your own collar.

Kabir's salok turns the same way and follows it all the way down: look at your own part first, so carefully that you run out of energy for judging anyone else. The second line matters as much as the first.

teach.h: WHOEVER SEES IT SO IS MY FRIEND.
teach.b: Whoever sees it this way is my friend. It's the ground of a friendship: two people who've both stopped pointing.

teach.h: WE ARE NOT GOOD, NO ONE IS BAD.
teach.b: Guru Nanak, in Raag Suhi, says we are not good, and no one is bad. Not crushing yourself; just taking yourself off the judge's bench.
The salok says I am the worst, but the line it hands us is the other half: everyone else is good. The point isn't a low opinion of yourself. It's the generous eye it frees up for everyone else.

how: Sikhs read and sing Kabir's saloks, gathered near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to teach nimrata, humility, alongside the Gurus' own hymns.

o: a prayer of asking, said while standing
a short verse, usually a two-line couplet
a long hymn sung at the end of a service

games.q: I am the worst of all — tap the pairs.
p: I am the worst; everyone else is good
whoever sees it so is my friend
we are not good, no one is bad

s: Sikh teachers read this salok as self-hatred
they hear humility: taking yourself off the judge's bench.
the salok has a second line about friendship
whoever comes to see it this way is my friend.
Kabir's saloks are scattered at random through the Granth
they're gathered together near the back of the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: you're Kabir, writing two short lines about faults. where do you point?
o: at the others, so they can improve.
at yourself: I am the worst, everyone else is good.
games.why: Kabir points in, and then adds: whoever sees it this way is my friend.

practice: Bring to mind one recent friction, an argument, a cold silence, a sharp text, and before you think about what they did, find your part, even a small one: a tone, a delay, an assumption.
Name it plainly, without punishing yourself for it, and notice how the other person looks once your part is on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be gentle.

wordCard.voice: Salok. Kabir's short couplet in the Guru Granth Sahib: apart from me everyone is good, and whoever sees it this way is my friend.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone else is good. Off the judge's bench, the eye grows generous. That's day seven hundred fifty-four.
